subject: maths
title: Time and Measurement
introductionText:
Term 1 · Measure
Time and Measurement
The Big Idea: We use time words to say when things happen, and length words to
compare how long things are. To compare lengths fairly, always start from the same line.
Say It Like This
Read aloud
"In the morning you wake up and have breakfast. In the afternoon you come home from
school. In the evening we have dinner. At night you sleep. Some things take a long time,
like sleeping. Some take a short time, like brushing your teeth. When we compare two
pencils, we put their ends on the same line. The one that sticks out further is longer."
Watch Out For
The slip almost every child makes
Comparing lengths without lining up the ends. A short pencil placed further along the
table "looks" longer. Always slide both to the edge of a book first, then compare.
Mixing up "long" and "tall". We say tall for things standing up (a person, a tree) and long
for things lying down (a train, a snake).
Try It at Home
Game 1 — Line them up (5 minutes)
Take three spoons — a teaspoon, a dessert spoon and a big serving spoon — and mix
them up. Ask him to guess the order from shortest to longest. Then line their ends against
the edge of a chopping board and check. Repeat with three pencils, then three shoes from
the door.
Game 2 — Long time or short time? (10 minutes)
Set a phone timer for one minute. How many times can he jump? Write his name? Then
compare: which takes longer — putting on his shoes, or eating a banana? Let him predict
first, then time both. Does the same job always take the same time?
morning afternoon evening night
wake up, breakfast home from school dinner sleep
longest
shortest
start line
Ask what he does at each time of day. Then cover the pencils and ask which is longest — uncover and check
against the start line.
More examples to talk about
• A blink is one of the shortest things we do; a night's sleep is one of the longest.
• Morning is before afternoon; evening is before night. The order never changes.
• A giraffe is tall; a train is long; a worm can be both short and long depending on what
you compare it with.
• Tricky: a curly piece of string can be longer than a straight one that looks longer.
Straighten it to check.
• Tricky: the longest pencil isn't always the heaviest or the newest.
Key Words
morning afternoon evening night before after longer shorter longest
shortest tall
